#4944. Taking Blood Pressure Meds? DASH Diet Likely Safe for Potassium Levels

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who adhere to the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet do not experience significant changes in potassium levels while taking blood pressure medications or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) drugs, according to a new study.

Researchers also reported that people taking these medications do not experience significant changes in their kidney function.

Both types of medications are known to increase potassium levels. High potassium levels can lead to hyperkalemia, a condition that can cause issues with the heart rhythm. People with impaired kidney function due to chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of hyperkalemia.

“The DASH diet is a well-known, proven nutrition pattern that is known to improve blood pressure,” said Marian Budu, MD, a clinical research coordinator on the GoFresh Trials at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston and the presenting author of the study, in a news release.

“Knowing that the DASH diet did not increase blood potassium levels in this population with normal baseline potassium levels provides assurance that the DASH diet can be prescribed to a wide range of people,” she continued.

The preliminary findings are being presented at the American Heart Association’s Hypertension Scientific Sessions 2026 meeting this week in Virginia. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the research provides medical professionals with important information.

“While we have traditionally exercised caution before recommending the DASH diet in patients who are prescribed ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, or potassium-sparing diuretics, these results show that those patients could likely adopt the DASH diet without significant concern for harm,” said Cheng-Han Chen, MD, an interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA.

“DASH diets do not appear to increase potassium levels to any significant degree in patients taking medications that are known to potentially raise serum potassium,” added Kevin Volpp, MD, the founding director of the Penn Center for Health Incentives and Behavioral Economics in Pennsylvania and the scientific lead of the American Heart Association’s Health Care by Food initiative.

“This is important because it is a theoretical concern that diets rich in potassium could cause high levels in potassium in some patients.”

The new study was a secondary analysis of the GoFresh and GoFresh Rx randomized trials that enrolled Black adults in the greater Boston area with high blood pressure.

Some of the participants were taking medications to lower their blood pressure, and others were not taking any hypertension drugs.

The study focused on four classes of blood pressure medications: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and potassium-sparing diuretics and beta-blockers, as well as NSAIDs.

The analysis took place in 2026 and included 356 Black adults with an average age of 53. About 70% were women.

At the start of the study, the participants had systolic blood pressure readings between 120 mm Hg and less than 150 mm Hg. They also had a diastolic blood pressure reading of less than 100 mm Hg.

The participants also had varying degrees of kidney function. In addition, they had limited access to grocery stores.

Half of the participants received three months of weekly DASH-patterned groceries and weekly nutrition counseling sessions. The other half received a cash stipend every four weeks to buy groceries, with no nutrition counseling.

The participants’ blood potassium levels were measured at the beginning of the study and again after 12 weeks.

The researchers reported that eating more potassium-rich foods in the DASH diet did not increase potassium levels to dangerous levels among participants taking blood pressure medications.

They noted no significant increase in potassium levels, regardless of whether participants were assigned to the dietary intervention or the monetary stipend group.

In a news release, the researchers acknowledged that their study did not include people with stage 4 or stage 5 kidney disease or those with higher-than-normal potassium levels.

They added that the study population comprised only Black individuals living in Boston, so the results may not generalize to the broader population.

The study authors said that future research should focus on participants with suboptimal kidney function and those with higher potassium levels.

Volpp agreed that more research is needed.

“This study was conducted in patients with non-elevated potassium levels at baseline and does not answer the question of whether they are safe in patients with elevated potassium levels or significant impairments in renal function,” he told Healthline.

Chen noted that potassium levels should be taken seriously.

“Certain classes of blood pressure medications can potentially cause high potassium levels, especially in people with kidney disease,” he told Healthline. “If potassium levels become too high, this can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, and muscle pain, or even serious heart problems such as arrhythmias.”

The DASH diet is a dietary plan that emphasizes fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins such as chicken, fish, and beans.

The plan also includes whole grains, low fat dairy products, and cooking with vegetable oils. The diet discourages the intake of red meat, salt, fat, and added sugars.

Previous research has indicated that the DASH diet can provide numerous health benefits.

A preliminary 2022 study concluded that the dietary plan can help lower blood pressure and improve heart health, but those results haven’t been published in a scientific journal. Still, the findings were consistent with a 2019 study that found the DASH diet can help lower the risk of heart disease.

In addition, a 2020 study reported that adults aged 65 and older with obesity lost body fat while following the DASH Diet. A 2023 study suggested the diet can help reduce belly fat.

A 2019 meta-analysis suggested that the DASH diet may also help lower the risk of certain cancers.

Many of these protective effects are attributed to the diet’s high fruit and vegetable content.

Chen said the DASH diet has many benefits, but the eating plan might not be for everybody.

“The DASH diet has been shown to be beneficial in lowering blood pressure, losing weight, and controlling blood sugar and cholesterol levels,” he said. “However, the amount of planning and portion tracking required to follow the diet may be too much for some people.”

Chen recommended that people ease into the DASH diet.

“The best way to start on the DASH diet is to slowly introduce the changes to your meals,” he said. “This can be as simple as including a few extra servings of fruits and vegetables each day as well as swapping some whole grain products for refined grains. Over time, more of the diet can be incorporated.”

Volpp agreed that introducing the DASH diet in increments is a good strategy.

“For many people, it is easiest to make small incremental changes sequentially,” he said. “One way to get started is to increase fruit by a couple of servings a day. Another is to pay attention to the amount of sodium in packaged foods and consciously choose products lower in sodium. A third is to make a conscious effort to eat more vegetables.”

“Make changes first that are easiest for you to make; it will be easier to make those changes stick,” Volpp added.

#4940. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: Lung Cancer Can Look Like Anyone

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Picture someone with lung cancer. Now picture a 24-year-old soccer player in the prime of his life. A filmmaker in her early 40s with a camera in her hand, doing what she loves best. A busy mom of two, with a shoulder so sore she can’t pick up her newborn, yet struggling to get a diagnosis.

The gap between the picture in our heads and the people actually being diagnosed is costing time. And time is the one thing with lung cancer you cannot get back.

We know that lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide and the leading cause of cancer death. And while lung cancer incidence rates are falling in many countries as fewer people smoke, lung cancer in people who have never smoked is on the rise globally, both as a proportion and in absolute numbers.

According to the CDC, as many as 20% of lung cancers diagnosed in the US are in people who have never smoked. Data suggests that non-smoking lung cancer is now among the most common causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide.

The numbers are stark. Lung cancer can affect anyone. And that includes the young – like Alex, one of the subjects of a powerful new short documentary commissioned by the charity EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK for their Our Lungs: Time to Breathe campaign.

Alex was a 24-year-old soccer player who died just weeks after receiving a diagnosis of Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) positive lung cancer, following several misdiagnoses born of the fact that no one suspected lung cancer in one so young, fit, and with no smoking history. The film was made by filmmaker Sarah Li, who herself was diagnosed with Stage 4 EGFR+ lung cancer in April 2024, just a month after Alex died from the same mutation of the disease, and charts her journey with survivor’s guilt, what an earlier diagnosis may have meant for Alex, and what that fact means for her own future.

Ahead of Lung Cancer Awareness Month in November, I sat down with my friend, Gini Harrison, to talk about the film, her own journey, and why catching lung cancer sooner matters so much. Gini is a Professor of Psychology at The Open University, a trustee of EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK, and is living with stage 4 EGFR-positive lung cancer. She’s also the mom at the top of this piece, whose sore shoulder was initially attributed to breastfeeding posture.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Gini Harrison: I’d had my son, Michael, in February 2021 and was on maternity leave. My daughter, Emily, was five. I think the shoulder pain started around March, but that was it. No cough, no breathlessness… nothing that made me think about my lungs.

Initially, they gave me painkillers, which helped a bit. But the pain kept getting worse. Eventually, I started losing movement and strength in my arm, and it got to the point where I couldn’t pick up my son anymore.

This was all happening during COVID, so my appointments were over the telephone. Eventually, after months without being examined face-to-face, I paid to see a shoulder specialist. As soon as he touched my shoulder blade and I practically leaped out of the chair, he knew something wasn’t right. He ordered an MRI, which showed a tumor in my shoulder blade and another in my upper right lung. In December 2021, I was diagnosed with stage IV lung cancer.

Gini Harrison: I wasn’t thinking, “This must be cancer.” I was just thinking, “Why isn’t this getting better?”

And I think that distinction matters. Patients shouldn’t have to identify their own disease before they can get help. You should be able to say that something is wrong and be listened to.

Gini Harrison: It was devastating. So many of my first questions were about the children: “How are we going to tell them?” “Am I going to be here to see them grow up?” “Will they remember me?” Suddenly, there was a question mark over a future I’d taken for granted.

I was also completely shocked by the type of cancer. If someone had said breast cancer, I don’t think I would have been anywhere near as surprised. But lung cancer?! I’d always associated it with smoking, and I’d never smoked.

I hadn’t imagined that this particular cancer could ever happen to me. So yes, I had some assumptions that I now challenge. I understand how deeply rooted they are because I had them too.

Gini Harrison: People are often shocked, and one of the first questions is whether I smoked.

And they often look healthy. That doesn’t mean everything is easy, or that there aren’t side effects. It just means you can’t tell what someone is dealing with by looking at them.

I think we’ve given lung cancer such a narrow public image that people outside it can become almost invisible.

Gini Harrison: Oh, yes! Once, I spoke to a doctor about a breathing problem after radiotherapy. He asked, “How much did you smoke?” When I said I’d never smoked, he replied, “Well, how did you get lung cancer then?”

On another occasion, I went to a hospice for help managing side effects, and someone there asked, “How are you still alive?” That’s quite a thing to hear when you’ve come looking for support!

When people ask about smoking, I try to explain that I’ve never smoked and I’m certainly not alone. Never smoking doesn’t make you immune. But I’m also very clear that nobody deserves lung cancer, whether they’ve smoked or not. We shouldn’t be creating a hierarchy of who deserves compassion.

Smoking history matters medically. But in a personal conversation, “How are you doing?” is a much kinder place to start.

Gini Harrison: Lung cancer isn’t one single disease. Two people can both have lung cancer, but different changes in their cells may be driving it.

Genes contain the instructions that tell our cells how to work, including when to grow and divide. Changes in those genes (called mutations) can cause cells to keep dividing when they shouldn’t, forming a tumor. In my case, there’s a mutation in a gene called EGFR.

EGFR-positive lung cancer is a type of non-small cell lung cancer caused by a genetic mutation in the EGFR gene, which keeps the EGFR receptor switched “on,” leading to uncontrolled cell growth and enhanced cancer cell survival.

Biomarker testing looks for these changes, as well as other features of the cancer that can guide treatment. If we know what’s helping the cancer grow, there may be a medication that specifically targets it.

The word “genetic” can sound scary, particularly when you have children. But these changes usually develop in cancer cells over a person’s lifetime. They aren’t necessarily inherited.

Gini Harrison: Please get it checked. And if it persists, worsens or doesn’t improve with treatment, go back. Explain what’s changed and how it’s affecting your life. Ask, “What happens next if this doesn’t get better?”

The symptoms don’t always look like lung symptoms. Mine was shoulder pain.

Most symptoms will turn out to be something other than cancer. But when a symptom continues to worsen, the original explanation needs to be reconsidered. Lower risk doesn’t mean no risk.

And I don’t want all the responsibility to fall on patients to keep pushing. Reassurance should come with a next step.

Gini Harrison: Once I had recovered from my initial treatment, I realized that I wanted to help others in my situation, so I became a trustee of the charity EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK. Through this work, we produced a film, Our Lungs: Time to Breathe. At the heart of it, it challenges the perception of what someone with lung cancer looks like.

The hardest part is how close to home it feels. Alex was so young, and that worked against him. Watching his family talk about what happened is heartbreaking. It’s just so unfair.

Gini Harrison: Sarah’s story shows life continuing alongside lung cancer. She’s a filmmaker with ambitions, people she loves, and things she wants to do.

Through Alex’s family, you see the enormity of the loss. I hope people feel that, rather than simply hearing another statistic.

Gini Harrison: For me, the biggest thing is that my children are growing up and I’m here to see it. Michael is now five (the age Emily was when I was diagnosed), and Emily is about to turn ten. I can’t tell you how grateful I am to be here with them.

It wasn’t about big bucket-list things. It was about being here every day. Seeing Michael start school. Seeing Emily reach double figures. Those milestones are enormous when you’ve wondered whether you’d get to see them.

After chemotherapy and radiotherapy, I’ve had no evidence of disease since May 2022, and my scans remain stable. But a big change has been seeing the progress in available treatment. It gives me more hope about what might be available if I need treatment again.

The public image of lung cancer still needs to catch up. We need better recognition of symptoms, access to appropriate testing and treatment, and support for the whole person. As a psychologist as well as a patient, I’m particularly aware that psychological well-being and family life need attention alongside the cancer itself.

Gini Harrison: I’d love for people to share the film and help get it in front of those who wouldn’t normally think lung cancer has anything to do with them. And take something from it into everyday life: book the appointment you’ve been putting off, ask your doctor about testing, or respond with kindness when someone tells you about their diagnosis.

Just being willing to rethink your assumptions could make a difference.

Gini Harrison: “You don’t have to put a brave face on with me. How are you really doing?”

When you look well, or your scans are good, people can assume you’re “fine now”. But I’m not sure the fear ever completely goes away. Every scan is terrifying. It feels like there’s a sword of Damocles hanging over my head, and part of me is waiting for the bad scan. I also still have lasting side effects from treatment, and probably always will.

My life has fundamentally changed. Some of that has brought good things, but it doesn’t make the difficult parts disappear. It helps when someone gives you room to be honest about both, without expecting you to reassure them or turn everything into a positive story.

Gini and I have been friends for nearly 30 years, and, while she’d probably cringe to hear me say it, I remain in awe of the way she approaches life with cancer. I am so grateful for her sharing her experiences with me for this column. What Gini asks of us is simple: look again, ask the question, listen, and act on your instincts. Our Lungs: Time to Breathe is where that starts for her. You can learn more about the Our Lungs: Time to Breathe campaign and the wider work of EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK by clicking the links. — Robin Hough

#4939. Scientists Were Shocked to Discover Yet Another Surprising Benefit of Cranberry Juice

Cranberry juice is known in certain circles as a helpful way to prevent the risk of future UTIs, but there's more to this beverage than that. Now, new research suggests the drink could also help your teeth...or at least help reduce plaque associated with tooth decay.

The study, which was published in the journal Scientific Reports, found that 100 percent cranberry juice could slow the growth of dental plaque and reduce the production of certain acids that could lead to cavities.

It's important to stress that the findings are preliminary at this point. But dentists say the idea of using cranberry juice to lower the odds of tooth decay isn't as out there as it seems. Here's the deal.

Meet the experts: Mark S. Wolff, DDS, PhD, dean at the University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine; Christine D. Wu, PhD, lead study author and professor in the Department of Pediatric Dentistry at the University of Illinois Chicago; Julie Meyerson, DMD, a dentist in New York City; and Matthew J. Messina, DDS, clinical associate professor at The Ohio State University College of Dentistry

For the study, researchers recruited 22 people (eight adults and 14 kids) and randomly assigned them one of three drinks: unsweetened 100 percent cranberry juice, cranberry juice cocktail (made up of 27 percent juice and added sugar), or water.

The participants didn't brush their teeth the morning of the experiment. To start, researchers collected dental plaque samples that had accumulated overnight with cotton swabs. The participants then rinsed their mouths with water, before having three small amounts of their assigned drink, swishing each around their mouths several times before swallowing.

After 30 minutes, the researchers took plaque samples again. (This time, they took samples from teeth that hadn't been swabbed earlier.) The researchers discovered that people who swished with and drank pure cranberry juice had slower plaque regrowth than those who didn't use the drink.

The pure cranberry juice was also linked with less acid production in dental plaque. (The acids made by oral bacteria can break down tooth enamel and increase the risk of cavities.)

Again, the study was small, so much more research is needed. And though the decision to study cranberry juice for oral health seems random, there's some precedent, according to Christine D. Wu, PhD, lead study author and professor in the Department of Pediatric Dentistry at the University of Illinois Chicago. "[Cranberry juice] has a polyphenol chemical compound called proanthocyanidin," she says. During research on the compound, Wu says her team discovered that proanthocyanidin can impact dental plaque.

"These compounds may interfere with processes involved in plaque formation," says Julie Meyerson, DMD, a dentist in New York City. For example, bacteria like Streptococcus mutans produce enzymes that convert dietary sugars into sticky substances called glucans, which help bacteria attach to teeth and form plaque biofilms, she says. "Cranberry polyphenols may interfere with these processes, making it more difficult for bacteria to adhere and form mature biofilms on teeth," Meyerson says. (That biofilm is also known as plaque.)

Cranberry compounds may also influence the metabolism of bacteria and reduce acid production as a result, she says. "This is important because acids produced by plaque bacteria lower the oral pH, contributing to enamel demineralization and tooth decay," Meyerson says.

Matthew J. Messina, DDS, clinical associate professor at The Ohio State University College of Dentistry, agrees that the proanthocyanidins are likely fueling this link. "These are the same compounds associated with cranberry’s reputation for urinary tract health," he says. "Proanthocyanidins don’t so much kill bacteria as interfere with them."

What we don't know right now is how this will actually impact dental health. "It could very well suppress plaque, but will it affect disease?" says Mark S. Wolff, DDS, PhD, dean at the University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine. "The findings are very preliminary."

Wu says that cranberry juice "may be a functional food" for dental health, but more research is needed.

Messina agrees. If you like cranberry juice, he recommends having unsweetened 100 percent juice over a cranberry juice cocktail. But at the same time, "don’t trade your toothbrush for a juice glass," he says. " Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between teeth, limiting sugar, and seeing your dentist regularly are still what prevent cavities."

#4937. 7 Best Oushak Rugs Fit for Royalty, Vetted by AD (2026)

Few home furnishings can make an ordinary room feel quite so grand as Oushak rugs. Named for the Turkish town of Uşak, where the weaving tradition began, these hand-knotted floor coverings gained popularity during the Ottoman Empire and were eventually exported across Europe. Their designs are recognizable for their large-scale medallions, geometric borders, and floral motifs, many of which drew inspiration from Ottoman art and architecture. The result is a style that’s decorative but never overly fussy, which helps to explain how it has withstood the test of time.

An Oushak rug can sit comfortably beneath a traditional dining table, add some contrast to a pared-back living room, or bring some personality to an otherwise neutral bedroom. And while antique examples are certainly worth seeking out, plenty of modern Oushak rugs capture the same old-world grandeur. Put simply, you may not be a sultan, but you can certainly decorate like one.

This one-of-a-kind, 100% wool rug is hand-knotted in Taşpinar, Turkey. Its intricate pattern, light pink palette, and low-pile height of half a centimeter give it a lived-in feel that works particularly well alongside more contemporary furniture. The wool is naturally durable, so even with a little wear, the rug has plenty of life left in it.

Bring a little more floral to your floors with this lavender Oushak. Its vintage-inspired pattern is full of the botanical motifs that make Turkish rugs so distinctive, while the soft color protects its relaxed aura from feeling overly ornate. Hand-knotted from New Zealand wool, the floor covering adds just enough pattern to a room without taking over. Basically, it’s the kind of rug that makes you want to kick off your shoes and stay awhile.

This cotton-candy-hued Oushak rug, another flower-filled masterpiece, features scattered palmettes and geometric shapes that draw on the rich history of Turkish patternmaking. Handmade by artisans in India from a blend of New Zealand wool, cotton, and polyester, and available in a variety of sizes to fit many spaces, the rug’s plush feel and storied patina make it a beautiful foundation for any room.

This Oushak-inspired rug pairs symmetrical designs with a sky-blue palette, bringing brightness to any room. Think of it as artwork you can touch or, rather, walk all over. Simply place it down and let the compliments roll in. It’s meticulously handwoven from high-quality wool, making it a durable choice for high-traffic areas, and because it comes in several sizes, its an especially versatile choice.

If you’re searching for a floor covering that has the essence of an antique Persian rug, but you aren’t quite ready to worry about spills, look no further. While this option features a delicate floral pattern, its tufted polyester construction makes it a more resilient selection for the busier corners of your home. It’s machine washable up to the 8-foot-by-10-foot size (larger versions are still washable but may require a commercial machine), and is available in area rug, round, and runner formats. It’s a particularly good pick for busy households where a beautiful rug has to do more than just look pretty.

For those who prefer more subtle patterns, this simple but sophisticated hand-knotted Oushak rug is a lovely option. Its understated mix of cream, brown, green, and blue complements a soft, slightly faded finish that gives it the appeal of a vintage find.

This Oushak rug looks like it belongs to another millennium and should live in the Metropolitan Museum of Art with its perfectly faded medallion pattern and ornamental border. But it’s actually brand new—and an affordable option for just about any home. Its muted palette can skew bohemian or coastal, or simply bring a little intrigue to a cozy space of any style.

#4936. The 89 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 16 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4934. The Fan Traditions You Need to Know This NWSL Postseason

The 2026 NWSL playoffs kick off on Friday, with single-elimination play that's guaranteed to be a nail-biter. Eight teams made the playoffs, but only one will hoist the championship trophy on November 21.

Of course, part of the fun of watching any playoff game is knowing insider-y details about each team. That includes fan traditions that make a team unique—and that you can join in on, too.

Every team has its own special chants and traditions that are uniquely theirs, and knowing what they are before kickoff immediately creates a level of familiarity you wouldn't have otherwise. You may already have "your" NWSL team that you root for, and you're probably familiar with their special traditions. But there are also likely teams you'll be watching during playoffs that you don't know the ins and outs of.

Whether you're looking for another club to root for when yours isn't playing or you just want to brush up on the details, these are the unique and sometimes hilarious fan traditions to know this NWSL postseason.

The San Diego Wave fans aren't messing around. They've formed their own supporters' group called the San Diego Sirens, and they're happy to include everyone in the club.

The Sirens have an online breakdown of songs and chants to know ahead of games. They even included helpful clips, so you can learn the melodies ahead of games. (There's a lot of water-themed content in there, making these very on-brand.)

The Utah Royals' fandom is called the Throne, and they march into the stadium as a united front before kickoff. (The Throne also says that everyone is welcome to join in.) The Royals also list their go-to chants online, allowing fans new and old to brush up before games.

Cloud 9 is Gotham's supporters club, and they've borrowed a few traditions from the UK's Manchester United. That includes incorporating John Denver’s “Take Me Home, Country Roads,” and making it “Gotham Roads,” as a tribute to the team.

You can download the club's songs on your phone and take them to the game or to your watch party to follow along.

The Royal Guard is Seattle Reign's fan club, and they've got plenty of traditions to share. The group does a walk toward Lumen Field before kickoff and incorporates a match-day band that might be the largest in NWSL. Check out their chants—with emojis to show when to clap—to get in the spirit.

The Kansas City Current has three different groups of supporters to make game day a high-energy event. That includes the KC Blue Crew, Surface Tension Drumming Club, and Undertow KC.

The organizations work together and have an online list of chants, the music they're set to, sheet music for drummers, and even videos to help fans get up to speed.

Not to be outdone, Angel City has six recognized supporter groups to cheer on its team—the most in the NWSL. Those groups regularly pack “La Fortaleza,” the supporters section. The groups share chants, and you can brush up on them online.

Rebellion 99 is Angel City's largest supporter group. Along with the other groups, they do chants and set off flares to keep the energy going. Rebellion 99 even has a scholarship program for local youth, stressing the importance of community-buildin

Washington Spirit offers four different fan clubs to choose from. One of the team's major groups, called the Spirit Squadron, marches to the stadium together before games. They also hilariously have a chant that they stole from the English Premier League called "Let’s pretend we scored a goal" when things aren't going so well.

There's also a stadium tradition: At the 51st minute, a "Free D.C." chant starts as a nod to the push for Washington, D.C., to become the 51st state.

The Portland Thorns' support groups are the Rose City Riveters and Timbers Army. They have a slew of chants you can download to follow along. In the mix: A chant called "Rose City 'Til I Die," which they do when the other team scores.

#4933. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

#4930. The Liver Does a Lot for Your Body. Here Are 8 Ways to Return the Favor.

Skip the herbal detoxes and follow these doctor-backed tips instead.

YOUR LARGEST INTERNAL organ is a master at multitasking. You can think of it as a refinery. Everything you consume—from your breakfast burrito to any medication you take—your liver filters, processes, stores, and/or turns into something new (it even makes cholesterol). The organ also puts in the hard work of regulating glucose, which involves holding on to that sugar and then deploying it when your body needs energy. And your liver helps handle the dirty work of sending whatever you don’t need out into the toilet.

ALL OF THE FACTORS below get in the way of your liver doing all of its jobs—and eventually prevent it from doing any of them. These drive the first stage of liver disease, which is inflammation. The second stage is called fibrosis, which occurs when chronic inflammation leads to liver scarring. In the third stage, cirrhosis, the refinery starts to function less efficiently. When cirrhosis goes too far, your liver begins to shut down, and eventually you’ll need a liver transplant.

The five main types are lettered A through E. In North America, A, B, and C are the most common, but A is typically mild. You used to hear a lot more about hepatitis B and C because they can lead to cirrhosis and even cancer—but they’re not the threat they once were (see more about that below).

Technically, your liver dies a little bit every time it processes alcohol. If you drink too much and kill too many liver cells, the liver has difficulty performing all its functions. Fat accumulates, and trouble is on its way.

Formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease is a fatty liver caused by things other than alcohol. The biggest culprits are obesity and type 2 diabetes. MASLD affects about 30 percent of people in the world, and cases are rising in the U.S.

YOU'LL NEED A doctor’s help. The severe symptoms you associate with liver problems—including yellowing eyes and skin (jaundice), swelling of the abdomen, or confusion—show up only when your liver is failing, says Richard Sterling, MD, hepatologist at Virginia Commonwealth University. Earlier symptoms, like fatigue, are so vague that liver trouble is tough to self-diagnose. A standard comprehensive blood panel, like the one you get with your annual physical, can measure the health of your liver and indicate a possible problem. The tests check liver enzymes (high is bad), platelet count (low is bad), albumin (you want high), total protein (low is bad), and bilirubin (high isn’t great). The panel should also include screenings for hepatitis B and C.

“WHEN PATIENTS COME to see me, they’re really scared,” says Rohit Loomba, MD, director of the MASLD Research Center at UC San Diego, because they think liver trouble is a death sentence. That’s not true anymore. “In the last two decades, we’ve completely revolutionized the treatment of liver problems,” Dr. Loomba says. Four positives:

Fibrosis that hasn’t advanced all the way to cirrhosis can be reversed, starting with removing the cause of the problem (by improving diet, avoiding alcohol). Even cirrhosis can be stabilized under the care of a liver specialist.

Better screening plus vaccines for hepatitis A and B have made viral hepatitis less common. Now there are good drugs for hepatitis B and ones that can basically cure hepatitis C.

The FDA approved Rezdiffra, the first drug for treating an advanced stage of MASLD called MASH, also formerly NASH. (Don’t ask.) And everyone’s favorite wonder drugs—GLP-1 inhibitors—may swoop in here too: Dr. Loomba published research that shows taking Mounjaro for a year was effective in treating MASH. Other semaglutide drugs might also work. In 2025, the FDA approved the use of Wegovy to treat MASH in adults with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis.

All cancers are scary, but liver cancer is one that may be preventable. For the most part, you only develop the disease once you’ve done extensive damage to the organ. If you get screened when you need it and adjust your lifestyle to keep your liver happy, you can limit your cancer risk.

Lean protein. Lots of produce. Little sugar. All easy on the liver.

A recommended 150 minutes per week at moderate intensity can help reduce liver inflammation and rid the organ of fat.

Antioxidants and other compounds in coffee (even decaf) may help protect against fibrosis. While studies may vary, researchers suggest positive effects start at two to three cups a day.

If you’re carrying extra pounds, losing 5 to 10 percent of your body weight could reduce fat in your liver by about 30 percent. Need some help? Check out MH’s four-week walking for weight loss plan.

Consume too much and your body converts it to fat that can build up in your liver. (This 30-day plan helps you cut back painlessly.)

Don’t stop taking them, but work with a doc to determine which ones can hurt your liver, especially if you’re drinking alcohol. Watch acetaminophen too: Even when taken as directed, it can cause liver damage if you drink to excess, says Dr. Sterling.

The best amount of alcohol for your liver: none. Realistically, though, when you drink, keep it to one or two and try not to do it daily. Note: Larger bodies can’t necessarily handle more. People with extra weight likely already have some liver damage that makes their body worse at processing booze.

These are unregulated, and some can be toxic to your liver; kava and herbal weight-loss supplements are two of the worst. And by the way, a “liver cleanse” or “liver detox”? “That’s not something we as hepatologists recommend,” says Dr. Sterling, “and I’m not aware of any data that say that that works.”

Kevin is a writer and editor living in Brooklyn. In past lives he’s been an economist, computer salesman, mathematician, barista, and college football equipment manager.

#4929. I Just Spent a Week in Iceland—Here's the Cold-Weather Capsule Wardrobe I'd Pack Again

The versatile staples and cozy essentials that made it into my suitcase.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I recently got back from a bucket-list trip: seven adventurous days in Iceland, chasing waterfalls, spotting rainbows, hiking remote canyons, and exploring the buzzy streets of Reykjavík. And while I may have perfected my travel capsule wardrobe, I’ll admit packing for Iceland was unlike any other destination.

I visited in late October, when temperatures hovered between 25 and 40 degrees Fahrenheit, though the wind often made it feel even colder. Iceland's weather can change dramatically throughout the day, so packing warm base layers and waterproof outerwear is essential. Between hiking to waterfalls, exploring the city's shops and restaurants, and long days in the car stopping at all the cool sights along the way, I needed clothes that could fend off wind, rain, sleet, and snow while regulating my body temp during everything from cool to freezing temps. But that didn’t mean sacrificing the gorpy-meets-girly outfits I wanted to wear (I am a style writer, after all).

Our first full day was a road trip from Reykjavík to Vík, which featured a beautiful string of waterfalls (or fosses, as they're called in Icelandic). It was a magical day, but also an incredibly wet one—so I was glad I'd packed plenty of waterproof gear. I walked behind the cascading water at Seljalandsfoss, took in the sheer scale and misty air of Skógafoss (which you might recognize from Game of Thrones), and fell particularly hard for Kvernufoss, a quieter waterfall tucked into a canyon that ended up being my personal favorite.

I ended up checking a large suitcase to make room for all my options—which is something I seldom do. (Not my smartest move, considering Icelandair charges a pretty penny for checked luggage!) In hindsight, I could have gotten away with much less if I'd been more strategic. So, I urge you to learn from my overpacking.

Ahead, I'm sharing the cold-weather capsule wardrobe I'd pack again for Iceland, including the waterproof essentials, versatile layers, and comfortable footwear that earned their place in my suitcase.

Weather can shift from bright and sunny to rainy and windy multiple times per day—and then you have the waterfalls to contend with, which will certainly have you soaked. So, a lightweight waterproof jacket is essential. Because I am extra, I packed three, but one or two is probably the magic number. The three coats below are the ones I actually wore: the water beaded right off all of these coats, and they were also super cute paired with my waterproof pants.

To go with your waterproof jacket, you’ll want at least one solid pair of waterproof, lightly insulated pants. You’ll have a base layer on underneath, so the pants don’t need to be too warm, but I think a plain shell pant might leave you feeling a bit chilly in the colder, rainier seasons. I brought three pairs of pants with me, but the two pairs below are the ones I would wholeheartedly pack again.

Halfdays Genevieve Gore-Tex 2L Insulated Pant

Initially, I thought a snowboot would be my most-worn shoe, but the conditions this time of year in southern Iceland made a waterproof hiking shoe more appropriate. If you visit in true winter or head further north, a snowboot might be your best bet. I recommend looking at the typical weather patterns for the region and time of year you're visiting, and keeping an eye on the forecast in the weeks and days leading up to your departure.

My trusted Merrell Moab 3 Mid waterproof boot ended up being perfect for our daily explorations, whether that involved misty waterfalls or moderate hiking. I also packed the Moonboot Icon Low as a snow boot option, and while they were undeniably stylish (and super warm), they weren’t the most useful for my particular visit. (They will certainly be my warm winter boot of choice this year, though!)

Warm wool socks are essential to wear under your hiking boots, not only for keeping your feet warm but also to help wick away moisture when things get sweaty. I wouldn’t skimp on socks—I brought six pairs (one for each active day of the trip).

Farm to Feet Damascus Merino Wool Crew Socks

When it comes to layering for winter or any cold-weather destination, base layers are key. These thermal tops and leggings help manage moisture to keep you warm and dry. I brought three sets, switching them out every two days, but if you’re keen to save more space, you could make do with two sets.

Iceland is not the place to rely on one chunky sweater to keep you warm. I found that having a few midweight wool sweaters and layers gave me much more flexibility, especially when temperatures and wind conditions changed throughout the day. Merino wool is particularly useful because it's warm and moisture-wicking without feeling overly bulky, making it easier to layer under a jacket.

I also brought a packable down jacket and a fleece to wear underneath my waterproof shell on especially cold days (or as an outer layer on warmer, drier days). Think of these as the middle layers in your outfit: You want enough warmth to stay comfortable, but enough flexibility to add or remove pieces as the weather changes.

I'd prioritize a warm, weather-resistant parka or winter coat for Iceland. If you opt for a fully waterproof parka (like the Finissterre Syke Waterproof Parka I brought with me), this can be your primary everyday coat. I personally preferred a lightweight shell jacket over my mid-layer for my daily adventures, though. But I liked having a longer jacket that provided extra coverage and warmth when I wasn't actively hiking—like while standing outside scanning the sky for Northern Lights or wandering downtown Reykjavik at night.

Look for something with a hood, a water-resistant or waterproof exterior, and enough room to accommodate a sweater or fleece underneath. Bonus points for something stylish enough to wear around the city without feeling like you're headed on an expedition.

Columbia Suttle Mountain Long Insulated Jacket

A warm beanie, insulated gloves, and a neck warmer or scarf might not feel as important as your sweaters and jackets, but you'll be grateful to have them when you're standing outside in the wind. I was particularly glad to have waterproof gloves and a warm hat on waterfall days and during our boat tour on the ice lagoon, when the combination of cold temperatures and misty spray made everything feel even chillier. I packed a few different options to go with my different outfits, but you could stick with one solid hat, scarf, or balaclava, and a pair of gloves to save space (though I was glad to have my chic leather gloves in Reykjavik!).

If you have one of the country's famous geothermal pools, hot springs, or lagoons on your itinerary, make room for a swimsuit and flip-flops. I visited Sky Lagoon, and though you can rent a swimsuit at most of the popular spots, having my own swimsuit along with a pair of easy slip-on shoes made the whole experience much more comfortable. These also take up practically no room in your suitcase, so this is one category where I wouldn't bother trying to cut back.

While most of my Iceland wardrobe revolved around technical layers and waterproof gear, I was glad to have one pair of regular pants for exploring Reykjavík. The city has a much more laid-back, everyday feel than some of the more rugged stops on the itinerary, and I didn't want to wear hiking pants to dinner or while popping into shops and cafés. A pair of jeans or casual travel pants is an easy way to feel a little more like yourself when you're off the trails. Just make sure they're comfortable enough for plenty of walking.

#4927. The 9 Most Walkable Cities in the US

Anyone who’s been to the pump lately could appreciate a little less reliance on cars. And while life in the most walkable cities in the US can mean saving on gas (not to mention car insurance, parking, and potential parking tickets), getting around on foot isn’t only about your budget. Walkability “can benefit everything from household finances and health to the environment and overall quality of life,” says Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin, which has been following and analyzing walkability for years with their Walk Score tool. “There’s also a housing-market component: People tend to value the convenience and access that comes with living in a walkable neighborhood, and that desirability can translate into high home values. Walkable neighborhoods also create more opportunities for people to interact with local businesses, use public spaces and resources, and connect with their neighbors,” says Fairweather.

To determine the country’s most walkable cities, we’ve reviewed recent studies, like the one from Only in Your State, a travel and discovery platform, plus talked to realtors, residents, and tourism experts across the country.

Hoboken is located on the banks of the Hudson River.

Just across the Hudson River from Manhattan, Hoboken is the most walkable city in the US, according to Only in Your State’s most recent analysis. The one-square-mile-city earned a nearly perfect Walk Score of 97, thanks to its dense street grid, many mixed-use buildings, and abundance of public transportation. Three other cities in the Garden State also cracked the list’s top 10: Union City, West New York, and Jersey City.

Though LA isn’t known for being particularly pedestrian friendly, West Hollywood remains a walkable enclave.

Los Angeles County isn’t known for its public transit, but even so, West Hollywood snagged the fourth spot in Only in Your State’s analysis, earning a Walk Score of 91. The city packs over 300 restaurants, bars, and coffee shops into just under two square miles. West Hollywood’s walkability is especially prized because the area is one of LA’s most vibrant nightlife districts, creating safe accessibility for revelers on the world-famous Sunset Strip.

In addition to being one of the country’s oldest, Boston is also one of the most walkable cities.

“What makes Boston special is that every neighborhood has its own personality and you can experience so much of the city on foot,” says George Sarkis, CEO and cofounder of the Sarkis Team at Douglas Elliman. “You can walk from the historic brownstones of Beacon Hill to the boutiques and restaurants of Back Bay, through the Public Garden, and into the South End without ever feeling like you’re covering much ground.” Walking is the best way to truly enjoy all of the city’s historic sites, centuries-old architecture, and cobblestone streets.

San Francisco’s hilly landscape can turn a casual stroll into an all-in workout.

This Bay Area city has one of the highest transit scores in the country, making it a breeze to go car-free. But for many locals—like Wendy Newman, a realtor with Wesely & Associates and a resident since 1987—walking is the real experience. “​​In one outing, you can buy groceries, stop for coffee, admire a Victorian’s unreasonable paint palette, nod at the neighbor whose face you know but whose name you still haven’t learned, and discover a bookstore you weren’t looking for,” she says. Plus, San Francisco’s mild climate makes taking a spin through neighborhoods like Chinatown and North Beach enjoyable year round.

New York City is built on a grid system, making it easy to navigate.

Just about every expert we talked to mentioned NYC, a metropolis made for a good stroll. From the café-lined lanes of Little Italy to particularly scenic stretches like the East River Promenade and Brooklyn Bridge Park, the Big Apple is big on pedestrian access. And the city’s high walkability score has benefits beyond just saving on cab fare, points out Kate Wollman-Mahan, a real estate agent at Christie’s International Real Estate New York. “Life expectancy in New York City is five years longer than the national average, according to the city-run Health Dashboard and economist Jonathan Miller (82.3 years versus 77.3 years),” she says. “Walking is built into everyday life, from going out to coffee to running errands to walking in the park.”

A stroll around DC can take pedestrians past national monuments and charming townhouses.

According to Walk Score, a research platform that promotes walkability, DC has a walk score of 98. It's such a popular pedestrian playground that even local cultural institutions embed walking into their education approach. Take the Spy Museum, for example, which developed its own free walking tour because of the breadth of strolling space in the area and interest from both residents and tourists. “We send them around the National Mall and downtown area with espionage history that happened in those exact places throughout history,” says Aliza Bran, the museum’s director of media relations. Other particularly walkable neighborhoods include Dupont Circle, U Street, Capitol Hill, and Georgetown.

The Windy City is a certified walking city.

The Windy City tops the US ranking for walkability from Preply, a language learning marketplace that runs walkability studies across the US, Europe, and Asia. “You can walk between Chicago’s five most-visited attractions (the Art Institute, Millennium Park, Cloud Gate, the Chicago Architecture Center, and the Magnificent Mile) in 28 minutes, about 2,500 steps,” says Preply’s communications leader Madeline Enos.

Sheldon Bishop, the founder of BrewAtlas, a guide to independent specialty coffee shops, argues that the best sign of a walkable neighborhood is a good cafe. And Chicago is particularly well caffeinated, thanks to 95 specialty cafes across 41 neighborhoods. “When people can walk to get coffee, they run into neighbors, stop into the bookstore next door, and spend money on the block instead of at a drive-thru,” he says.

Miami is full of walkable pockets, according to local residents.

For Sandra Masis, director of sales at the residential building Arbor Coconut Grove, it’s neighborhoods like Coconut Grove that make Miami such a pedestrian-friendly city. “You can walk to restaurants, cafés, shops, parks, and the waterfront, all while enjoying the neighborhood’s lush greenery and relaxed atmosphere,” she says. “It has a sense of community that makes you want to get outside and explore.” And Miami’s newer developments, like Brickell, prioritize walkability as much as older neighborhoods like Coconut Grove and Little Havana. “Even in a city built around cars, you can create pockets where people can comfortably live, work, and socialize on foot,” says Masis.

Contemporary high-rises mingle with historic sites in Philadelphia.

Every year GuruWalk, a platform for free tours, puts together a ranking of the best cities in the world to explore on foot. In their most recent study, NYC took the top spot among US cities, and Philadelphia came in just behind it. GuruWalk’s Carolina Martínez says that though Philly gets fewer visitors than other places on the list, those who explore it love it. “Philadelphia has a 4.99 average rating, with 99 percent of reviews at five stars,” she says. “Walk a few blocks through the historic district and you’re standing in front of Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell.” New Orleans, San Francisco, and Boston round out the top five.
